title: 自动驾驶激光雷达与视觉
full_query: Write a concise technical report exploring why some autonomous vehicle systems prioritize LiDAR while others rely on neural networks and cameras.

pointwise.title: Why prioritize LiDAR
pointwise.question: Does the report state a concrete system-design rationale for prioritizing LiDAR?

anchors.1: No rationale or a fundamentally false choice claim.
anchors.2: Only calls LiDAR accurate or safe.
anchors.3: Names a useful capability but does not connect it to the system's perception need.
anchors.4: Connects a concrete capability to the system need, with a minor scope ambiguity.
anchors.5: Clearly connects LiDAR capability to a stated perception/design need and explains why that benefit matters for this priority.

pointwise.boundary: Coverage of hardware variants, pipeline, compute, latency, energy, cost and mitigation is checked in05–14, not repeated here. This item asks why the stated capability motivates the choice, not how many constraints were listed.

query_quotes: why some autonomous vehicle systems prioritize LiDAR
provenance.change_note: v3.3 targeted revision: Remove integration-cost and limitation completeness from old high anchors; these are now direct independent content objects.

pointwise.title: Why prioritize cameras and learning
pointwise.question: Does the report state a concrete system-design rationale for prioritizing cameras and learning?

anchors.1: No rationale or an inherently sufficient-for-safety assertion.
anchors.2: Only says cheap or human-like.
anchors.3: Names a benefit but does not connect it to the system's perception or deployment need.
anchors.4: Connects a concrete camera/learning benefit to the system need, with a minor scope ambiguity.
anchors.5: Clearly explains why the visual information or learned-perception capability motivates the chosen priority for a stated system need.

pointwise.boundary: The detailed inference pipeline is05 and deployment economics11; do not penalize their omissions here again. Camera depth need not be purely learned; no fixed brand.

query_quotes: others rely on neural networks and cameras
provenance.change_note: v3.3 targeted revision: Remove repeated pipeline/data/cost completeness while preserving the distinct camera-choice rationale.

pointwise.title: Nonexclusive system architectures
pointwise.question: Does the report avoid treating LiDAR, cameras and neural networks as mutually exclusive alternatives?

anchors.1: Claims LiDAR systems do not use neural networks or cannot include cameras.
anchors.2: Builds the comparison on a sensor-versus-software binary despite a passing qualification.
anchors.3: Does not explicitly make the false claim, but the architecture relationship remains ambiguous.
anchors.4: Clearly recognizes LiDAR systems can use cameras and learning, with only minor ambiguous shorthand.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes sensor choice from perception software and explains that LiDAR-equipped systems can also use cameras and neural networks; the comparison concerns priorities or sensor suites rather than incompatible categories.

pointwise.boundary: Fusion-stage taxonomy is optional. Acknowledging coexistence does not require advocating sensor fusion.

query_quotes: LiDAR while others rely on neural networks and cameras
provenance.change_note: Make the central false-dichotomy risk a direct check; do not mandate early/late fusion.

pointwise.title: Limits relevant to sensor choice
pointwise.question: Does the report explain consequential limitations of both approaches and relate them to operating conditions?

anchors.1: Both are portrayed as reliable in all situations, or limitations are fundamentally reversed.
anchors.2: Only one side has a meaningful limitation, or both receive vague weather/AI labels.
anchors.3: Gives a concrete limitation for each side but does not connect it clearly to the choice.
anchors.4: Explains concrete environmental and generalization constraints for the compared approaches, with minor scope asymmetry.
anchors.5: Explains relevant sensing failure and learned-inference/generalization failure mechanisms, their operating conditions and consequence for reliable perception; neither approach is presented as universally reliable.

pointwise.boundary: Check failure mechanisms only. Mitigation, redundancy and fallback belong to12 and cannot be separately required here; no exhaustive weather/attack list. Each approach must have a meaningful limitation; either side absent scores2.

provenance.change_note: v3.3 targeted revision: Failure versus response can independently succeed; remove fallback from the old full-score anchor.

pointwise.title: Traceable comparative claims
pointwise.question: Can readers identify the basis for consequential empirical, manufacturer or numerical comparisons?

anchors.1: Main comparative claims have no identifiable basis.
anchors.2: Most consequential claims rely on vague authority or untraceable figures.
anchors.3: Key comparisons are attributable, but some important scope, model or date details are unclear.
anchors.4: Consequential comparisons have identifiable sources and contexts with minor gaps.
anchors.5: Empirical or industry-specific comparisons are tied to identifiable sources, systems and relevant conditions/dates; conceptual reasoning is clearly distinguished from empirical claims.

pointwise.boundary: Do not require manufacturers, numerical benchmarks or URLs. A conceptual report can satisfy this through identifiable technical grounding and clearly bounded reasoning.

provenance.change_note: Local audit for fast-changing system comparisons, not a mandatory benchmark.

pointwise.title: Support in the checked sample
pointwise.question: Do actually checked sources support the sampled claims about sensors and perception systems?

anchors.1: The sample contains fabricated evidence or contradictions central to the comparison.
anchors.2: Several consequential sampled claims exaggerate or misstate the evidence.
anchors.3: The sample has mixed support with a material correction needed.
anchors.4: Sampled claims are supported apart from minor context or wording errors.
anchors.5: Every claim in the stated sample is supported at its actual system, task and operating scope, without turning a perception metric into proven whole-vehicle safety.

pointwise.boundary: Only judge an actual documented verification sample. Failed retrieval is an execution problem, not a low score or NA; disclose unverified scope. Do not require numeric claims solely to make an audit possible.

provenance.change_note: Separate source support from traceability and evidence selection.

pointwise.title: Perception and downstream interfaces
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how LiDAR measurements and camera inputs become perception outputs used by the driving stack?

anchors.1: No sensor-to-perception account.
anchors.2: Only names point clouds, images or neural networks.
anchors.3: Explains one input path but not the other, leaves the processing of an input at the level of algorithm names, or leaves the downstream prediction/planning interface unclear.
anchors.4: Explains both representations, processing and downstream use with minor detail missing.
anchors.5: Explains how LiDAR range/geometric data and camera images are processed into relevant perception outputs, and how those objects or scene estimates inform prediction or planning; clearly distinguishes measurement and inference in the routes described.

pointwise.boundary: No mandatory SLAM/segmentation roster, exact neural architecture or monocular learned-depth route. Explain substantive processing for both LiDAR and camera inputs rather than merely naming neural networks. Learned monocular depth, stereo/temporal geometry or other relevant camera-perception routes are eligible; where depth is discussed, distinguish the method actually described and do not claim all camera depth is purely learned. PT.D1.01/02 check the choice rationale, not this pipeline again.

provenance.change_note: Review 35: remove mandatory learned monocular depth from levels 3/5 and boundary; retain substantive processing of both sensor inputs and downstream use. Official exact monocular-depth omission detection is not preserved.

pointwise.title: LiDAR implementation differences
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how relevant LiDAR design variants change the comparison rather than treating LiDAR as one uniform device?

anchors.1: No recognition of consequential hardware variation.
anchors.2: Only says solid-state or advanced LiDAR.
anchors.3: Names a variant contrast but not its effect on measurement or integration.
anchors.4: Explains a concrete design contrast and consequence with minor conditions missing.
anchors.5: Explains a relevant scanning, ranging or packaging contrast and its measurement/integration tradeoff, making clear why the claimed LiDAR advantage depends on implementation.

pointwise.boundary: No exhaustive wavelength/detector catalogue or mandatory emerging technology. A concrete architectural contrast is needed, not a brand list.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Fusion and integration choices
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how combining information at different processing stages changes system tradeoffs?

anchors.1: No integration-stage explanation.
anchors.2: Only says sensors can be fused.
anchors.3: Identifies a stage choice but not the representation or consequence, or assumes fusion always improves accuracy.
anchors.4: Explains a meaningful early/intermediate versus late integration contrast with a relevant tradeoff.
anchors.5: Explains where representations are combined and how that choice affects information use, modularity, alignment or processing burden, without a universal accuracy ranking.

pointwise.boundary: No required terminology or fusion implementation. 03 only checks nonexclusive sensor/software categories; coexistence is not this stage explanation.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Compute requirements
pointwise.question: Does the report explain the drivers of computational workload for LiDAR and camera perception?

anchors.1: No compute discussion.
anchors.2: Only calls an approach computationally heavy.
anchors.3: Explains compute for one side only, or gives an unqualified universal scaling law.
anchors.4: Explains both sides' important data/model workload drivers with minor assumptions missing.
anchors.5: Relates image or point-cloud volume, temporal processing and model/integration choices to compute on both sides, with conditions rather than assuming linear scaling or one universally cheaper pipeline.

pointwise.boundary: No FLOP target or mandatory full variable list. Compute operations, elapsed latency and energy are different objects; do not reuse one missing detail to penalize all three.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Latency and action timing
pointwise.question: Does the report explain latency tradeoffs from sensing through perception to timely action?

anchors.1: No latency discussion.
anchors.2: Only says fast or real time.
anchors.3: Identifies a delay but not its consequence for driving or the relevant pipeline conditions.
anchors.4: Connects sensing/processing delay to update or reaction needs, with minor assumptions missing.
anchors.5: Explains how sampling, accumulation, processing or fusion delays affect usable scene freshness and response time under the compared conditions, distinguishing throughput from end-to-end latency.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed millisecond threshold; hardware and workload context matter. Low FLOPs alone do not establish low latency.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: System energy requirements
pointwise.question: Does the report distinguish sensor power and processing energy in the LiDAR-camera comparison?

anchors.1: No energy discussion.
anchors.2: Only calls one approach energy efficient.
anchors.3: Discusses sensing or computation energy but omits the other, or uses sensor power alone as total system power.
anchors.4: Explains sensing and processing contributions for the compared systems with a minor operating assumption missing.
anchors.5: Explains active illumination/sensor power and computing/integration demand as distinct contributors, bounding the comparison by configuration and duty cycle rather than declaring a universal winner.

pointwise.boundary: No exact watts or fixed sensor/compute ranking required. Do not infer power directly from FLOPs without implementation context.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Deployment economics
pointwise.question: Does the report explain acquisition and integration/operation costs that influence sensor priorities?

anchors.1: No cost rationale.
anchors.2: Only says LiDAR expensive or cameras cheap.
anchors.3: Discusses hardware price or lifecycle/integration burden but omits the other or its relevance to deployment.
anchors.4: Explains both cost levels and why they matter for the proposed system, with minor scale/context missing.
anchors.5: Relates sensor procurement and integration/calibration/maintenance or data-compute burden to deployment scale and design priorities, without equating cheap sensors with a cheap full system.

pointwise.boundary: No dollar threshold or required Tesla example; one-sided cost descriptions cannot pass by naming a brand. 01/02 no longer separately require cost coverage.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Mitigation and fallback
pointwise.question: Does the report explain responses to sensing/inference failures and the limits of redundancy or fallback?

anchors.1: No response to failure.
anchors.2: Only says use AI or more sensors.
anchors.3: Explains a mitigation or residual-failure response, but omits the other or discusses only one approach without addressing the other system's failure response.
anchors.4: Addresses mitigation and residual-failure handling for both compared approaches, with a minor common-cause or operating condition missing.
anchors.5: Explains responses to relevant sensing and inference failures for both approaches and how redundancy, degraded operation or safe fallback handles residual uncertainty, including shared environmental or learned-model failure limits.

pointwise.boundary: No prescribed de-weathering method, laser wavelength or hardware redundancy. 04 checks failure mechanisms only; do not repeat absent mitigation there.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Safety assurance and deployment rules
pointwise.question: Does the report explain how safety assurance and regulatory/deployment conditions affect sensor selection?

anchors.1: No assurance/deployment-constraint account.
anchors.2: Only says safety or regulation matters.
anchors.3: Mentions testing or regulation without explaining the constraint on selection, or treats one modality as automatically compliant.
anchors.4: Explains assurance requirements and deployment/operating restrictions with minor scope detail missing.
anchors.5: Explains why operating-domain evidence, failure handling and applicable deployment approval/audit requirements constrain the choice, distinguishing performance metrics from an accepted vehicle-level safety case.

pointwise.boundary: No fixed jurisdiction, legal citation or claim that law mandates LiDAR. Rules may be discussed conditionally with scope stated; this is technical-report coverage, not legal advice.

provenance.change_note: Restore a substantive technical domain previously left optional or only in broad PW; specific implementations remain replaceable.

pointwise.title: Published like-task performance comparison
pointwise.question: Does the report provide an identifiable published quantitative comparison of LiDAR-based and camera-only systems on the same perception task?

anchors.1: No empirical comparative result.
anchors.2: Only a dataset name, modality slogan or proposed future experiment; no reported comparison.
anchors.3: A quantitative result is supplied, but a system, task, metric, source or important comparison condition is unclear or mismatched.
anchors.4: Named systems, task, source and interpretable quantitative results are present, with minor condition details missing.
anchors.5: Presents sourced quantitative results for identifiable LiDAR-based and camera-only systems on a comparable task, explaining configurations, metrics and limits on attributing the gap to sensor choice.

pointwise.boundary: No new experiment or fixed benchmark/model pair is required. Do not invent unavailable numbers. A proposed protocol alone is not a published result and cannot earn 4/5. A well-justified result limitation can be explained but does not count as supplying the missing result.

provenance.change_note: Main-agent v3.5: restore a published-result check; a proposed protocol no longer substitutes for empirical evidence.
